report:
## Conclusion

Evidence has shifted from skepticism to cautious support. Early large trials, including a well-designed placebo-controlled RCT in 319 college women (Barbosa-Cesnik et al., 2011), found conventional cranberry juice did **not** significantly reduce recurrent UTI/cystitis risk. However, this and similar negative trials often used low-dose juice with inconsistent proanthocyanidin (PAC) content.

More recent, higher-quality evidence points the other way. The updated 2023 Cochrane systematic review (50 RCTs, ~8,857 participants) found cranberry products reduced the risk of symptomatic, culture-confirmed UTIs by roughly 26% overall, with the **clearest benefit in women with recurrent UTIs** and in children—though effect sizes were modest and heterogeneity across products was high (cobfoundation.org summary of Cochrane review). A 2024 meta-analysis (Frontiers in Nutrition) reinforced this, showing that cranberry products—particularly those with **high, standardized doses of PACs (≥36 mg/day)**—significantly reduced recurrence in women with a history of recurrent cystitis. A double-blind RCT comparing high- vs low-dose PAC extract also showed high-dose formulations were more effective (BMC Urology, 2018/2021).

**Bottom line:** Standard cranberry juice at typical commercial concentrations shows limited, inconsistent benefit. However, standardized cranberry extracts with a sufficiently high PAC dose (≥36 mg/day) taken regularly can modestly but meaningfully reduce recurrence of uncomplicated cystitis in women prone to recurrent UTIs. It is not a substitute for antibiotics in acute infection but may serve as a reasonable adjunct preventive strategy, especially for those wishing to avoid long-term prophylactic antibiotics.

**Sources:**
- https://academic.oup.com/cid/article-abstract/52/1/23/406427 (Barbosa-Cesnik et al., RCT, cranberry juice ineffective)
- https://cobfoundation.org/health-information/cranberry-vs-d-mannose-for-uti-prevention/ (summary of 2023 Cochrane review)
- https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2024.1422121/full (2024 meta-analysis, high-dose PAC efficacy)
- https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12894-021-00811-w (high- vs low-dose PAC RCT in women)
